paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis finds projections that capture shared variation between two sets of measurements. This paper introduces RSG+, a stochastic algorithm for extracting several such components efficiently. Its central move is to rewrite the projection matrices in a structured form, making the problem suitable for established optimization techniques on Riemannian manifolds.

The reformulation matters because previous approaches faced different computational compromises. Some required O(d³) work per iteration and converged at a rate of O(1/√t); others achieved O(1/t) convergence but extracted only the leading component. RSG+ combines O(d²k) work per iteration with O(1/t) convergence while extracting the top k components. Here, d is dimensionality and t counts iterations, so the result connects computational cost directly to how many components are requested.

The main contribution is the formulation and its theoretical analysis. Experiments on common datasets also show promising behavior, supporting the method's practical potential. The authors additionally explore its possible use in training fair models when protected-attribute labels are unavailable, presenting this as an application direction rather than an established general solution.
neurips-2021-an-online-riemannian-pca-fo.tldr: RSG+ reformulates canonical correlation analysis to extract multiple components with faster convergence and lower per-iteration cost than the compared approaches.

paragraphs: CCVS learns to create new video clips from existing ones while combining temporal continuity with user control. Its self-supervised approach conditions generation on both the surrounding video context and additional guidance. These inputs have complementary purposes: context helps successive frames belong together, while guidance specifies aspects of what the generated clip should contain or do.

The prediction process operates autoregressively in two spaces. A transformer forecasts future content in an autoencoder's latent space, while image-space updates refresh the context used for subsequent predictions. A learned optical-flow module uses this context to encourage consistency across space and time. Adversarial training addresses both individual appearance and temporal behavior, aiming to make the resulting clips more realistic.

A quantization stage connects the encoder to the forecasting transformer, with an inverse stage before decoding. This supports control through different kinds of information, including sample frames, audio, or image-space trajectories. It also permits multiple predictions to reflect uncertainty about the future. Experiments report strong qualitative and quantitative results across several tasks and standard benchmarks, supporting the combined approach to controllability and coherence.
neurips-2021-ccvs-context-aware-controll.tldr: CCVS combines contextual prediction, multimodal guidance, and consistency mechanisms to generate controllable video clips with multiple possible futures.

paragraphs: A useful video summary depends on what the viewer considers important. CLIP-It addresses this by letting natural language guide the selection of video content. The same framework handles summaries tailored to a user's query and generic summaries intended to represent the video more broadly, bringing together two tasks often treated separately.

The model uses a multimodal transformer to score frames. It considers both how important frames are relative to one another and how they relate to language. For a customized summary, that language comes from the user's query. For a generic summary, it comes from an automatically generated dense video caption. Language therefore provides a source of guidance even when a viewer has not supplied a request.

The approach can also be trained without ground-truth summary supervision. Reported experiments outperform baselines and prior methods on TVSum, SumMe, and the query-focused QFVS dataset. Particularly large improvements in transfer experiments support the authors' claim of strong generalization in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a shared mechanism for connecting visual importance with either explicit user interests or automatically described content.
neurips-2021-clip-it-language-guided-vid.tldr: CLIP-It uses language-guided frame scoring to produce both generic and query-focused video summaries within one framework.

paragraphs: Active inference describes agents that maintain an internal model of the world and act toward preferred outcomes. In this view, goals take the form of optimistic predictions the agent tries to fulfill. The paper investigates how to make this approach practical in complex environments, where learning the internal model and planning actions can be computationally demanding.

The proposed change is a contrastive objective for active inference. It substantially reduces the computational burden associated with both model learning and planning. This matters because the appeal of a self-supervised control objective depends on whether agents can actually learn and use it efficiently when observations are complex, including images.

In image-based tasks, the method performs substantially better than likelihood-based active inference while being cheaper to compute and easier to train. It also closely matches reinforcement learning agents that receive human-designed rewards. Further experiments show stronger performance for contrastive methods when distractors are present, and demonstrate that the proposed agent can carry goals across background variations. These findings support its usefulness for visual control without establishing that it replaces reward-based learning in every setting.
neurips-2021-contrastive-active-inferenc.tldr: A contrastive objective makes active inference cheaper and more effective on visual control tasks, with improved handling of distractors and background changes.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a sequence generator can produce outputs with stronger desired attributes than those represented in its training data. The focus is attribute extrapolation: generating beyond the training distribution along a property of interest. The authors formulate this as a task spanning both natural language and protein sequences, connecting two domains through the same generative challenge.

Their framework, GENhance, enhances attributes through a learned latent space. That space provides the representation through which generation is directed toward stronger attribute values. The relevant distinction is between reproducing the kinds of examples encountered during training and producing sequences whose target property extends beyond those examples. The framework is evaluated using movie reviews and a dataset of computed protein stability.

The reported results show generation of strongly positive reviews and highly stable protein sequences despite the absence of similar examples during training. The protein evidence is situated in the computed-stability dataset described by the authors. They also release benchmark tasks and models, providing resources for further work on extrapolative generation and data-driven design in biology and chemistry.
neurips-2021-deep-extrapolation-for-attr.tldr: GENhance uses a learned latent space to generate text and protein sequences with enhanced attributes beyond the examples encountered during training.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether entropy, a measure of uncertainty in a distribution, can be estimated with accuracy bounds determined empirically from observations. For arbitrary discrete distributions, that goal is impossible without additional assumptions. The authors identify an information-moment assumption that makes it feasible, including when the set of possible outcomes is infinite.

The assumption is central to the result. The authors describe it as natural and, in a qualified sense, minimal: it is weaker than requiring finite support or imposing tail-decay conditions. Under this assumption, they provide finite-sample entropy estimates for infinite alphabets that nearly attain known minimax rates. This connects practical estimation from a limited sample with theoretical benchmarks for achievable accuracy.

The empirical accuracy bounds are also reported to be substantially sharper than existing bounds for several natural distributions and meaningful sample regimes. A further theoretical contribution concerns continuity: how much entropy can change when distributions are close in total variation distance. Their dimension-free result extends a finite-alphabet continuity result, making the number of possible outcomes less restrictive in this analysis.
neurips-2021-dimension-free-empirical-en.tldr: An information-moment assumption enables empirical entropy accuracy bounds and near-minimax finite-sample estimation even for infinite alphabets.

paragraphs: DynamicViT starts from the observation that a vision transformer's final prediction often relies on only a subset of its most informative tokens. Processing every token through every layer can therefore spend computation on information that contributes little to the decision. The paper proposes removing redundant tokens progressively, with the selection adapted to each input image.

Lightweight prediction modules estimate token importance from the current features at several layers. This allows pruning to happen hierarchically as representations develop. To train these decisions end to end, the authors use attention masking: a token is differentiably pruned by blocking its interactions with other tokens. The resulting irregular token sets remain compatible with efficient computation because of how self-attention operates.

Across the evaluated vision transformers, pruning 66% of input tokens reduces FLOPs by 31–37% and increases throughput by more than 40%, with an accuracy drop within 0.5%. These measurements matter together: the method delivers actual processing gains alongside reduced arithmetic work. ImageNet results show competitive accuracy-versus-complexity trade-offs against contemporary convolutional networks and vision transformers.
neurips-2021-dynamicvit-efficient-vision.tldr: DynamicViT progressively removes input-dependent redundant tokens, substantially accelerating tested vision transformers with a small accuracy drop.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent reduces communication by allowing training nodes to average information only approximately. The difficulty is that cheaper communication per iteration can come at the cost of needing more iterations. This paper studies how the communication graph can improve both sides of that trade-off, making averaging effective without requiring extensive exchanges.

The authors analyze exponential graphs, where each of n nodes connects to O(log n) neighbors. They prove that these graphs support efficient communication and averaging together. They also identify a useful sequential property: a sequence of log n one-peer exponential graphs can achieve exact averaging collectively, even though each node contacts only one neighbor in an individual iteration.

Using these graph structures in decentralized SGD and momentum SGD yields the reported state-of-the-art balance between communication per iteration and iteration complexity among commonly used topologies. Experiments across multiple tasks and models support the prospect of fast, high-quality training. The key insight is that communication quality depends on how exchanges accumulate over time, allowing a sparse sequence of contacts to accomplish effective global averaging.
neurips-2021-exponential-graph-is-provab.tldr: Exponential communication graphs give decentralized training an efficient balance between inexpensive exchanges and effective averaging across nodes.

paragraphs: Stochastic bandit algorithms repeatedly choose among options whose reward distributions are initially uncertain. Many guarantees assume that those distributions belong to a known family or satisfy known bounds. This paper asks how algorithms behave when such information, especially about distribution tails, is unavailable or misspecified. Its goal is to connect strong performance under standard assumptions with robustness under broader ones.

The proposed Dirichlet Sampling framework compares options pairwise using empirical indices built by resampling their observations. A data-dependent exploration bonus supplements these comparisons. Different variants of this common strategy are analyzed under different distributional assumptions, allowing the method's guarantees to be matched to the information available about rewards.

For bounded distributions, variants achieve provably optimal regret. For semi-bounded distributions, logarithmic regret holds under a mild quantile condition. A simple tuning also provides robustness across a large class of unbounded distributions, with asymptotic regret slightly worse than logarithmic. These results make the robustness trade-off explicit rather than claiming one guarantee covers every case. Numerical experiments on a synthetic agriculture decision problem illustrate the approach's merits.
neurips-2021-from-optimality-to-robustne.tldr: Dirichlet Sampling offers resampling-based bandit strategies that trade distribution-specific optimality for broader robustness with a modest regret penalty.

paragraphs: Incorrect labels and uneven class frequencies can occur together in real datasets. Existing weighting approaches address these problems by changing how strongly each training example contributes, using a small clean and unbiased dataset for guidance. This paper argues that assigning one weight to an entire example overlooks useful distinctions among its class-level learning signals.

Generalized Data Weighting, or GDW, applies the chain rule to separate the loss gradient into class-level components. It then weights those components independently. This provides finer control over learning: the influence associated with one class can be adjusted separately from other class contributions within the same example. The method is designed to address label noise and class imbalance simultaneously.

The authors obtain these class-level weights through a gradient-descent step that uses intermediate gradients. They report no extra computational cost compared with instance-weighting methods, making the finer control practical in the evaluated comparison. Experiments across multiple settings support its effectiveness. In one stated example, GDW improves over state-of-the-art methods by 2.56% on CIFAR10 with 60% uniform label noise.
neurips-2021-generalized-dataweighting-v.tldr: GDW separately weights class-level gradient contributions to combat label noise and class imbalance without reported extra cost over instance weighting.

paragraphs: A neural network can learn to generate adversarial perturbations, providing a faster alternative to optimizing a new perturbation through a more expensive procedure. This paper examines whether such generators remain effective when their deployment conditions differ from training. It studies transfer across target network architectures, target datasets, and target tasks, making generalization of the attack itself the central question.

The proposed approach focuses on intermediate network representations. The authors identify these mid-level features as shared ground across the different architectures, data, and tasks they consider. They then build a loss function around those features to train a perturbation generator. The motivation is to target representations that carry relevance across settings, helping the learned perturbations transfer beyond their original training conditions.

Experiments show the approach outperforming the compared state-of-the-art universal and transferable attack strategies. The finding supports mid-level features as a useful basis for learning transferable perturbations in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the work separates the speed advantage of generative attacks from the distinct question of whether their effectiveness survives changes in what they attack.
neurips-2021-learning-transferable-adver.tldr: Training perturbation generators with a mid-level feature loss improves adversarial transfer across the evaluated architectures, datasets, and tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate an intervention's average effect from panel data when treatment can occur across a general pattern of entries. It models observations as three parts: an underlying low-rank matrix, zero-mean noise, and treatment effects added wherever a binary treatment matrix indicates intervention. Individual treatment effects are allowed to differ across entries.

The target is the average effect among treated entries. This distinction matters because the method is not required to recover every heterogeneous effect separately. The authors extend the synthetic-control framework beyond the setting where all treated entries lie in a single row. Allowing a general treatment matrix broadens the intervention arrangements that the framework can address.

Within the stated modeling setting, the paper provides rate-optimal recovery guarantees for the average treatment effect and describes them as the first guarantees of their kind in this general case. Computational experiments on synthetic and real-world data show a substantial advantage over competing estimators. The contribution combines broader treatment-pattern coverage with theoretical accuracy guarantees, while retaining the low-rank baseline and zero-mean-noise assumptions that define the problem.
neurips-2021-learning-treatment-effects-.tldr: The paper extends synthetic-control-style estimation to general treatment patterns, with rate-optimal average-effect recovery under a low-rank panel model.

paragraphs: Feature-based dynamic pricing requires a seller to price a sequence of differentiated products using their observed features. Decisions must be made as products arrive. Performance is measured by regret relative to an omniscient pricing strategy available in hindsight, so the objective is to limit the accumulated cost of learning while making pricing decisions.

The paper introduces EMLP for stochastic features and ONSP for adversarial features. Both receive optimal O(d log T) regret guarantees, where d is the feature dimension and T is the number of products. The earlier stochastic bound depended on the smallest eigenvalue of the feature second-moment matrix, which can approach zero, or on a square-root dependence on T. The earlier adversarial bound grew as T^(2/3).

A complementary lower bound shows that a slightly more general setting requires at least order √T regret. Together, these results identify knowing the demand curve as decisive for the stronger logarithmic guarantee. The improvement therefore belongs to a specific informational setting: the paper both establishes efficient learning there and demonstrates a harder nearby case where comparable regret is impossible.
neurips-2021-logarithmic-regret-in-featu.tldr: Two pricing algorithms achieve optimal O(d log T) regret, while a lower bound shows why knowing the demand curve is crucial to this improvement.

paragraphs: Conventional data compression often aims to preserve how content looks to people. This paper considers data that will instead be consumed by predictive algorithms. Its question is how much information must be stored to preserve performance on relevant prediction tasks, even if the compressed representation does not retain all the information needed for perceptual fidelity.

The theoretical analysis characterizes the required bit rate for predictive tasks that remain unchanged under a specified set of transformations, such as data augmentations. That invariance defines which distinctions matter to the target task family. The authors use the resulting theory to construct unsupervised objectives for training neural compressors, connecting a statement about information requirements to a practical learning procedure.

A generic image compressor trained with these objectives achieves substantial rate savings relative to JPEG across eight datasets without reducing downstream classification performance. On ImageNet, the reported savings exceed 1000-fold. The result concerns preservation of predictive performance, and the theoretical scope is the transformation-invariant task family. Together, the theory and experiments show how compression can be organized around what algorithms need to predict.
neurips-2021-lossy-compression-for-lossl.tldr: Task-aware compression objectives yield major image bit-rate savings while preserving measured downstream classification performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural networks that represent learning procedures themselves. Its Variable Shared Meta Learning framework, or VSML, brings together ideas including fast weights, Hebbian plasticity, learned update rules, and meta recurrent networks. The central claim is that simple patterns of weight sharing and sparsity are sufficient to express powerful learning algorithms in a reusable form.

In a concrete implementation, ordinary network weights are replaced by tiny LSTMs. This construction can implement the backpropagation learning algorithm through forward execution alone. The distinction is about how the learning computation is represented and run: a recurrent neural mechanism can carry out a procedure normally associated with explicit backward gradient calculations.

VSML can also meta-learn algorithms that differ from online backpropagation and operate without explicit gradient calculation. The authors report that these learned procedures generalize to datasets outside the meta-training distribution. Inspection suggests that they learn through rapid association in a way qualitatively different from gradient descent. These results show that the framework can express a familiar algorithm while also discovering different learning behavior, rather than merely reproducing a fixed update rule.
neurips-2021-meta-learning-backpropagati.tldr: VSML uses shared, sparse neural computation to express backpropagation and meta-learn alternative learning algorithms that transfer beyond their training distribution.

paragraphs: Neural networks can forget earlier tasks when training on a new task overwrites useful weights. MARK addresses this by encouraging reusable knowledge across a sequence of tasks. It maintains shared weights as a common knowledge base that supports new learning and is enriched as additional tasks arrive.

Two mechanisms organize that knowledge base. A meta-learning procedure incrementally incorporates new knowledge and encourages weights to remain useful across tasks. Trainable masks then select which shared weights each task should use. These components address complementary needs: building reusable representations and giving individual tasks access to the parts relevant to them.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. On 20-Split-MiniImageNet, MARK exceeds the best-performing compared methods by over 10% in average accuracy, with almost no forgetting while using 55% of the number of parameters. An ablation study provides evidence that the shared knowledge is genuinely reused and selectively accessed by tasks. The findings support the method's intended mechanism as well as its measured performance, linking retention and parameter efficiency through selective reuse.
neurips-2021-optimizing-reusable-knowled.tldr: MARK combines a meta-learned shared knowledge base with task-specific masks to improve continual learning through selective weight reuse.

paragraphs: Covariate shift occurs when training and test inputs follow different distributions while the conditional relationship between inputs and labels stays the same. This paper analyzes that problem for random-feature regression in a high-dimensional limit. It derives precise limiting expressions for test error, bias, and variance, allowing the effect of a shift to be examined mathematically.

The analysis motivates a partial ordering of covariate shifts. This ordering gives a sufficient condition for deciding when a shift will worsen or improve test performance. A partial order need not compare every pair of shifts, and a sufficient condition does not claim to characterize every possible case. The result nevertheless gives a structured way to identify the direction of performance changes.

Within the analyzed setting, overparameterized models show greater robustness to covariate shift, supplying a theoretical explanation for an empirically observed pattern. The analysis also produces an exact linear relationship between in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization performance. These conclusions are tied to the random-feature model and high-dimensional asymptotics, where the paper can characterize the relevant errors precisely.
neurips-2021-overparameterization-improv.tldr: High-dimensional random-feature theory explains enhanced covariate-shift robustness from overparameterization and a linear relationship between in- and out-of-distribution performance.

paragraphs: PortaSpeech aims to generate expressive, detailed speech with a compact model. The design follows an analysis of two generative approaches: small variational autoencoders capture longer-range features such as prosody but can produce blurry, unnatural results, while normalizing flows reconstruct fine spectral details well but struggle when their parameter budget is restricted.

The model combines a lightweight variational autoencoder with an enhanced prior and a flow-based post-network supplied with strong conditioning. Grouped parameter sharing in the flow's affine coupling layers reduces model size and memory use. A linguistic encoder also combines hard word-level alignment with soft phoneme-level alignment, explicitly incorporating word-level meaning while reducing dependence on precise fine-grained text–speech alignment.

Experiments report better voice quality and prosody modeling than the compared text-to-speech systems under subjective and objective evaluations. Reducing PortaSpeech to 6.7 million parameters causes only slight degradation, with about fourfold model-size and threefold runtime-memory compression relative to FastSpeech 2. Ablation studies support each design choice. The findings show that combining complementary generative mechanisms can retain speech quality under a smaller resource budget.
neurips-2021-portaspeech-portable-and-hi.tldr: PortaSpeech combines compact prosody modeling, flow-based detail generation, and mixed text–speech alignment to produce high-quality speech with fewer resources.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning is appealing for sequential tasks because exact recursive updates and a single update using all observations lead to the same result. In practical deep models, however, inference must usually be approximated. Repeated approximation can produce poor compromises across tasks, weakening the theoretical attraction of applying ordinary Bayesian updating directly to continual learning.

Posterior meta-replay takes a different approach by continually inferring parameter distributions conditioned on the task. Its implementation uses probabilistic task-conditioned hypernetworks to represent these distributions. This changes what is retained across the sequence: the framework compresses a collection of task-specific posterior distributions, preserving different parameter possibilities associated with different tasks.

On standard benchmarks, the authors report virtually no forgetting of the represented posterior sequence and substantial gains over existing Bayesian continual-learning methods. They identify task inference as the main limiting factor: deciding which task is relevant remains difficult even when its parameter distribution has been preserved. Several causes of this difficulty are independent of sequential learning itself, suggesting that improving retention and improving task identification are distinct routes to further progress.
neurips-2021-posterior-meta-replay-for-c.tldr: Posterior meta-replay compresses task-conditioned parameter distributions with virtually no forgetting in benchmarks, while task inference remains its main limitation.

paragraphs: Predify investigates whether recurrent dynamics inspired by predictive coding can improve the robustness of image classifiers. The motivation is that strong classification accuracy does not give deep networks the resilience to input disturbances seen in human perception. The authors add a mechanism that lets a convolutional network repeatedly revise its internal representations.

At each level, generative feedback reconstructs the activity in the preceding layer. Differences between those predictions and the layer's activity provide reconstruction errors. These errors drive iterative updates across timesteps and train the feedback weights on natural images without labels. Prediction and correction therefore become part of how the network processes its representations, rather than classification relying solely on one feedforward pass.

Adding this strategy to VGG16 and EfficientNetB0 improves robustness against the evaluated corruptions and adversarial attacks. The authors hypothesize that other feedforward networks could benefit as well, keeping that broader claim separate from the two demonstrated cases. They release a PyTorch package, Predify, for adding and investigating these dynamics in convolutional networks, enabling further study of when recurrent prediction helps.
neurips-2021-predify-augmenting-deep-neu.tldr: Predify adds iterative predictive feedback to convolutional networks, improving VGG16 and EfficientNetB0 robustness against tested corruptions and adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated auction design with production costs for a buyer whose objective is to maximize total value while satisfying a return-on-investment constraint. That behavior differs from maximizing utility, where the objective is value minus payment. The distinction matters because the auction must account for a buyer pursuing value subject to a spending-related constraint, a model motivated by automated advertising bids.

The authors seek a prior-independent dynamic mechanism. Their performance comparison is especially demanding: the benchmark is the largest revenue a seller could extract if every buyer value were publicly known. Regret measures the mechanism's revenue shortfall relative to this fully informed benchmark over a horizon of T interactions.

The main result is a mechanism with regret bounded by Õ(T^(2/3)), where the notation suppresses logarithmic factors. Because this grows more slowly than T, the guaranteed benchmark shortfall per interaction decreases as the horizon grows. The contribution establishes a quantitative connection between prior-independent auction design and the first-best revenue target in the stated setting with production costs and a value-maximizing buyer.
neurips-2021-prior-independent-dynamic-a.tldr: A prior-independent dynamic auction achieves Õ(T^(2/3)) regret against fully informed revenue extraction for an ROI-constrained, value-maximizing buyer.

paragraphs: The paper studies safe reinforcement learning in environments where a short look ahead can reveal how to avoid unsafe states. This assumption defines the setting: near-future planning must be sufficient to steer away from danger. Within that setting, an agent with a sufficiently accurate model of the environment can use predicted consequences to support safer decisions.

The proposed model-based algorithm assigns heavy penalties to unsafe predicted trajectories. Planning therefore evaluates potential behavior with an explicit cost for entering dangerous states. The authors derive guarantees that the algorithm can avoid unsafe states under certain assumptions. These are conditional guarantees, tied to the setting and the requirements of the analysis rather than an unconditional promise of safe behavior.

Experiments on several continuous-control tasks show competitive rewards with fewer safety violations. This combination matters because safety is evaluated alongside the agent's ability to accomplish its task. The empirical result supports the practical value of short-horizon model-based planning in the tested environments, while the theory explains why accurate prediction can provide safety benefits when nearby hazards are avoidable.
neurips-2021-safe-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Penalizing unsafe predicted trajectories improves safety in tested control tasks, with conditional guarantees when short-horizon planning can avoid danger.

paragraphs: Computing graph similarity supports applications such as retrieval and anomaly detection, but exact measures such as graph edit distance are computationally difficult for large graphs. Neural approximations can compare graphs more efficiently. Their accuracy often benefits from allowing the graphs' features to interact early, although these dense interactions make each comparison slower.

The paper first builds an expressive teacher using co-attention to fuse graph-neural-network features at multiple levels. It then transfers the teacher's knowledge to a faster student. The student supports storing individual graph embeddings offline, so later comparisons can reuse those representations. This separates the expensive process of learning detailed comparisons from the repeated cost of performing them.

Knowledge transfer introduces an alignment problem because the teacher's joint embedding depends on both graphs. The authors address it by decomposing that dynamic representation into static pseudo-individual embeddings for teacher–student alignment. Experiments on real-world datasets show advantages in both accuracy and efficiency over compared methods. On the AIDS benchmark, the reported speedup over prior work exceeds tenfold, supporting distillation as a way to retain much of early fusion's accuracy at faster inference.
neurips-2021-slow-learning-and-fast-infe.tldr: A co-attention graph-comparison teacher trains a faster student with reusable embeddings, achieving strong accuracy and over tenfold speedup on AIDS.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation aims to improve classification in a target domain without target labels. A common strategy aligns source and target feature representations to reduce the effect of differences between domains. ToAlign questions whether aligning an entire feature representation is the right objective, since some of that representation may have little relevance to classification.

The method uses knowledge induced by the classification task to guide feature decomposition. It separates a source feature into a discriminative, task-related component and a task-irrelevant component. Alignment then focuses on the component that supports classification, while the irrelevant component is ignored. This makes the choice of what to align part of the task-solving process itself.

The distinction matters because domain similarity alone does not ensure that the aligned information helps distinguish classes. ToAlign explicitly directs alignment toward that purpose. Experiments across Office-Home, Visda-2017, and DomainNet, under different adaptation settings, demonstrate effectiveness and help achieve state-of-the-art performance. The reported results support using classification knowledge to select alignment targets rather than treating every part of a learned feature as equally useful.
neurips-2021-toalign-task-oriented-align.tldr: ToAlign improves unsupervised domain adaptation by aligning the classification-relevant portion of source features while ignoring task-irrelevant information.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks gain efficiency and accuracy by sharing weights across locations, but the paper argues that this mechanism is problematic as a model of biological neurons. Locally connected networks avoid literal weight sharing yet perform substantially worse. The authors therefore seek a more biologically plausible way to encourage similar responses to identical inputs across a pool of neurons.

They first consider training with multiple translations of each image, resembling changes in visual input caused by saccades. This requires many translations and does not close the performance gap. Their proposed alternative adds lateral connections to a locally connected network and uses Hebbian plasticity, with occasional sleep-like phases that encourage a functional analogue of weight sharing.

The resulting locally connected networks achieve nearly convolutional performance on ImageNet and fit ventral-stream data better. These findings support the idea that some benefits of convolution-like regularization can arise through a different learning mechanism. The method therefore offers a bridge between the practical success of convolutional networks and efforts to explain visual-system activity, while retaining the paper's framing as progress toward biological plausibility.
neurips-2021-towards-biologically-plausi.tldr: Lateral connections and sleep-like Hebbian learning bring locally connected networks close to convolutional accuracy while improving their fit to visual-system data.
